Removing the Thorn From the Rose:

How Best to Use LLMs
Aleks Stanic MD, PhD
Vice Chair for Research · Division Director of Reproductive Sciences, · Faculty, Reproductive Endocrinology and Infertility · Dept ObGyn UW-Madison
MRSi 2026 · Drake Hotel, Chicago · 28 July 2026 · @StanicLabUW · @UW_ObGyn · @UWMadison

Disclosures

None
Commercial LLM products are discussed/mentioned by necessity and open/free weights models added to discussion wherever appropriate

LLMs promise faster, fuller, less painful care.

Beware the thorns though.

The Red Line: What NEVER Enters the Context Window

Protecting Patient Privacy, Intellectual Property, and Institutional Integrity

Part 1

How do LLMs actually work?
Part 1

A next-token predictor, not a knowledge base

Models predict the next token, a sub-word unit, then re-feed and repeat; there is no fact retrieval, no knowledge database, only statistical completion of the sequence from the training distribution
3 training stages shape it toward specific reward objectives:
1) Pretraining minimizes prediction error across trillions of tokens
2) Alignment optimizes a reward model shaped by human preference rankings,
3) Specialization adds domain performance;
4) “Reasoning”: inference-time chain of thought improves outcomes
Part 1

A next-token predictor, not a knowledge base

Part 1

Inside the engine: attention and word order

Self-attention computes each word's meaning from its full surrounding context via query-key-value projections, so 'no evidence of malignancy' reads as a negative finding, not a flag on 'malignancy’
Multiple attention heads run in parallel, each capturing a different linguistic relationship (coreference, negation, temporal sequence), while positional encoding preserves word order
Part 1

Inside the engine: attention and word order

Part 1

Grounding: from pattern recall to citable answer

Grounding interposes a retrieval step before generation: the query fetches verified source text into the context window, and the model is constrained to generate from retrieved evidence and cite its span
The probability mass shifts toward tokens supported by the retrieved documents, so each claim arrives with a pointer to a verifiable source the reader can open
Checkable does not mean correct: if retrieval returns off-target documents, the model grounds confidently in the wrong evidence, and the citation reads as if it supports the claim; the source must still be read
Part 1

Grounding: from pattern recall to citable answer

Part 1

LLMs have anterograde amnesia

The base model does not update from your conversation; its weights are frozen at the training cutoff, so the correction you made today changes nothing in the model
Part 1

LLMs have anterograde amnesia

Persistence is re-injection, not learning
A "memory" feature is a separate store of short notes the app writes about you and quietly pastes back into the context window at the start of later sessions

Part 2

Scribes & chatbots in your clinic
Part 2

Ambient scribes: burnout relief?

Expert-equivalent drafts, nonzero residue
In a 10-physician blinded reader study, best-adapted LLM summaries were equivalent (45%) or superior (36%) to physician-written ones, with the expert preferred in only 19%
The model reduced but did not erase fabrication: misinterpretations, inaccuracies, and hallucinations in 6%, 2%, 5% of samples, versus 9%, 4%, 12% for the experts
Van Veen D, et al. Nat Med 2024;30:1134-1142. Adapted LLMs can outperform experts at clinical summarization. · Li W, et al. Sci Rep 2026;16:5607. Fine-tuned LLM discharge summaries.
Part 2

Ambient scribes: burnout relief?

Expert-equivalent drafts, nonzero residue
A separate fine-tuned model drafted each discharge summary in ~83 s versus the 30-50 min by hand, and 94% were rated EHR-acceptable after minor human verification
The caveat is operational: ~6% of audited drafts held a minor factual inconsistency, the timing excludes review and signature, and the legal responsibility stays with the clinician
Van Veen D, et al. Nat Med 2024;30:1134-1142. Adapted LLMs can outperform experts at clinical summarization. · Li W, et al. Sci Rep 2026;16:5607. Fine-tuned LLM discharge summaries.
Part 2

Your patients already ask the bots

Controlled accuracy is the easy half
ChatGPT-4 answered all 170 true/false PCOS-infertility items correctly, twice, 30 days apart; open-ended answers improved over the month (accuracy 5.53 → 5.88 of 6, p<0.001)
These are expert-graded knowledge, not patient outcomes; the study tested recall against guidelines, not what a patient does with the answer
The catch: both Copilot and Google answered above an 8th-grade reading level, exceeding the health-literacy ceiling for patient material
Devranoglu B, et al. Diagnostics 2024;14:1082. ChatGPT for PCOS-infertility queries. ·
Part 2

Your patients already ask the bots

Controlled accuracy is the easy half
Part 2

…but in real hands, reliability collapses

The model is fine; the handoff is not
In a randomized, preregistered trial of 1,298 adults, the same models alone identified the condition 94.9% of the time, but lay users with them identified a relevant condition under 34.5% and the right action under 44.2%
People using ordinary search did better on the safety-critical part: 1.57× higher odds of catching a red-flag condition than people using the LLMs
Bean AM, et al. Nat Med 2026;32:609-615. Reliability of LLMs as medical assistants for the public. · Draelos RL, et al. npj Digit Med 2026;9:241. LLMs give unsafe answers to patient-posed questions.
Part 2

…but in real hands, reliability collapses

The model is fine; the handoff is not
The failure is conversational: models offered 2.21 conditions per chat, only 34% correct, and users gave partial histories in 16 of 30 transcripts
Physician red-teaming of 888 answers found 5-13% outright unsafe; at ~43 million US patient questions a month, even 5% is millions of unsafe answers if those rates hold
Bean AM, et al. Nat Med 2026;32:609-615. Reliability of LLMs as medical assistants for the public. · Draelos RL, et al. npj Digit Med 2026;9:241. LLMs give unsafe answers to patient-posed questions.
Part 2

Sycophancy: the model wants to please you

Asked to justify switching a brand drug to its identical generic for new "safety" reasons, GPT-4o, GPT-4, and GPT-4o-mini complied 100% of the time (50/50); Llama3-8B 94%
This was not a knowledge gap: the setup first confirmed the models knew the drugs were the same, then showed they still aligned with the user's false premise
Chen S, et al. npj Digit Med 2025;8:605. When helpfulness backfires: medical sycophancy.
Part 2

Sycophancy: the model wants to please you

Asked to justify switching a brand drug to its identical generic for new "safety" reasons, GPT-4o, GPT-4, and GPT-4o-mini complied 100% of the time (50/50); Llama3-8B 94%
The mitigation is a prompt you can write: permission to refuse plus a factual-recall cue raised correct rejection to 94% for GPT-4 and GPT-4o
Prompting helps most when the user already suspects the flaw, so patient-facing systems need model-level guardrails, not just better bedside wording
Chen S, et al. npj Digit Med 2025;8:605. When helpfulness backfires: medical sycophancy.
Part 2

The sharpest thorn: skill drift

In early observational evidence, experienced endoscopists (avg 27 yr) saw unaided adenoma detection fall 28.4% → 22.4% after months of AI-assisted colonoscopy, a 21% relative drop
The implication is conditional but serious: that drop could translate to roughly 18% more missed colorectal cancers, given the link between detection and interval cancer
Automation bias spares no one: when mammography AI gave wrong reads, radiologist accuracy fell from ~80% to 20-46% by experience
Topaz M, et al. Ann Intern Med 2026. The deskilling effect. · Gong EJ, et al. Ann Intern Med 2026. The human factor in clinical AI.
Part 2

The sharpest thorn: skill drift

The generational risk is never-skilling: a trainee who only ever reasons with AI may never build the unaided framework for when it is absent or wrong
Mitigation is a manual mode: periodic AI-off practice and audit, the procedural skills most exposed in REI being embryo grading, ultrasound, and surgery
Topaz M, et al. Ann Intern Med 2026. The deskilling effect. · Gong EJ, et al. Ann Intern Med 2026. The human factor in clinical AI.
Part 2

The Red Line: decide what never gets pasted

The prompt box is a disclosure
Consumer tools (red): free or personal web apps carry no business-associate agreement, so de-identified questions and drafting only, never PHI
Enterprise no-train (amber): paid endpoints that contractually do not train on inputs lower the leak risk, but without a signed BAA are still not cleared for PHI
BAA-covered or on-prem (green): the only tier identifiable data may enter, and only for the approved use
Khanna S. Therap Adv Gastroenterol 2026;19:17562848261441693. Responsible use of LLMs: privacy & governance.
Part 2

The Red Line: decide what never gets pasted

The prompt box is a disclosure
Part 2

The Red Line: decide what never gets pasted

The prompt box is a disclosure
Under HIPAA, any vendor that handles ePHI needs a BAA even in "no-view" encrypted setups, and the "don't train on my data" toggle stops training reuse, it does not create a BAA
IVF data resists de-identification: PGT genetics, and partner linkage are inherently identifying, so the genome is the identifier
Khanna S. Therap Adv Gastroenterol 2026;19:17562848261441693. Responsible use of LLMs: privacy & governance.
Part 2

Running a clinical model inside your own walls

On-prem accuracy on two commodity GPUs
Quantization stores weights at lower precision (4-bit vs 16-bit), shrinking a model ~4× so it fits hardware a hospital already buys, with little measured accuracy loss on these benchmarks
A locally deployable clinical model (AIDx) reached 83.61% across nine MultiMedQA subsets, running fully on-premises in 28.1 GB across two RTX 4090 GPUs at 0.84 s per query
Alwakeel A. Sci Rep 2026;16:18172. AIDx: a locally deployable clinical AI.
Part 2

Running a clinical model inside your own walls

On-prem accuracy on two commodity GPUs
Most of the competence came from fine-tuning on de-identified EHR data (+17.8 points); retrieval added only +0.4 on exams
The cleanest Red Line for IVF: on-prem means embryo images, time-lapse, and PGT genetics are queried without PHI ever leaving the network
Caveat: this is a benchmark, not a clinic; no clinical or usability validation
Alwakeel A. Sci Rep 2026;16:18172. AIDx: a locally deployable clinical AI.
Part 2

A safer, verifiable chatbot prompt

Role: "You are a careful clinical assistant." A bounded role narrows the model off its confident-generalist default
Context: give it the question and what you already know, so the answer is grounded in your evidence, not the question alone
Rules: cite every source, flag uncertainty, and refuse to go beyond the evidence, so a missing citation surfaces instead of hiding in fluent prose
The Red Line: never paste PHI into a consumer tool; the same prompt that is safe with a de-identified vignette is a breach with a real one
Part 2

Personal System Prompt

You are an extremely capable, thoughtful, and precise scientific assistant (senior PhD expert level).
Your goal is to deeply understand the user's intent, ask clarifying questions when needed, provide clear and accurate answers, and proactively anticipate helpful follow-up information. Tell me if a request is illogical, wrong, or no data is available after tool-calls. Always prioritize being truthful, nuanced, insightful.
Writing style: Formal, professional tone, and writing style should be biased towards full explanations in clear language.
Sources: Use the widest variety of published literature in all scientific prompts, and always cite rigorously (citations at the end of response format). Cite seminal studies in addition to those that directly address the query and be biased towards multiple sources / citations. When citations are complete, re-read them and confirm against scientific databases. If there is no answer or the resource is not available, say so, do not invent plausible answers.
The whole thing is published verbatim: the full system prompt.

CONFIRM: When citations are complete, re-read them and confirm against scientific databases.
GIVE FAILURE MODE: If there is no answer or the resource is not available, say so, do not invent plausible answers.

Part 3

Agentic AI: LLMs taking action!
Part 3

From chatbot to agent

An agent adds a planning-and-execution loop around the language model: it formulates a step, calls an external tool (search, code interpreter, database), observes the return, and decides whether the task is complete or needs another cycle
The loop is the capability: the agent retrieves information absent from its training data, runs a computation rather than estimating it, and decomposes a complex problem into individually verifiable steps
The loop is also the liability: tool errors propagate across cycles, the context window fills with intermediate output until critical information is displaced, and unsupervised loops run indefinitely without converging
Part 3

From chatbot to agent

Part 3

Agents in medicine: modest gains, large tax

Planning and tools help, not enough
In the first systematic clinical-agent benchmark, the best agent lifted simulated diagnostic accuracy from 51.4% to 60.3% on one task and 24.0% to 28.0% on another, gains the authors call modest and often not significant
On hard medical questions the agent reached 30.3%, statistically indistinguishable from plain GPT-4.1 at 28.8% (p=0.871), so the architecture did not break the ceiling
Liu Y, et al. npj Digit Med 2026;9:259. Benchmarking LLM agent systems for clinical tasks.
Part 3

Agents in medicine: modest gains, large tax

Planning and tools help, not enough
The cost was disproportionate: ~11× the tokens and ~2× the latency on dialog tasks, up to ~100× the tokens on knowledge questions
Safeguards filtered 89.9% of hallucinations, yet hallucinations still affected ~30% of clinical scenarios; the authors call current agents not reliable for routine deployment
Liu Y, et al. npj Digit Med 2026;9:259. Benchmarking LLM agent systems for clinical tasks.
Part 3

Deep-Research mode: breadth at a price

When long runs help, and when they hurt
Deep-Research modes plan, search, and synthesize across many sources in one long run; they earn their keep on broad scoping, where coverage matters more than one exact value
Cost compounds: the long run carries the agent tax, more than 10× the tokens and 2× the latency, for the same modest accuracy lift
Liu Y, et al. npj Digit Med 2026;9:259. Benchmarking LLM agent systems. · Liu NF, et al. Trans Assoc Comput Linguist 2024;12:157-173. Lost in the middle.
Part 3

Deep-Research mode: breadth at a price

When long runs help, and when they hurt
Long inputs hide the answer: models use a fact best at the start or end of a context and worst in the middle, a U-shaped curve where mid-context accuracy fell below using no documents at all
The discipline: trust Deep-Research for map-making, then open the primary source and re-check any number a decision rests on
Liu Y, et al. npj Digit Med 2026;9:259. Benchmarking LLM agent systems. · Liu NF, et al. Trans Assoc Comput Linguist 2024;12:157-173. Lost in the middle.
Part 3

Part 3

The demo, in one loop: plan, fan out, verify

Plan first: the agent prints its sub-questions and study-design rules before it searches, so the reasoning is auditable, not hidden
Fan out: one subagent per sub-question, each fetching the primary PDF rather than a summary
Verify: a separate pass re-opens every source, and a claim the agent could not retrieve is not used; this is the same loop that vetted the literature in this talk

Recorded demo: Claude Code CLI reviews

fresh vs frozen embryo transfer
Recorded demo: Claude Code CLI reviews

Prompt

You are running a focused evidence review on FRESH versus FROZEN (elective frozen, "freeze-all")single embryo transfer in IVF, and then publishing it as a self-contained HTML explainer.
Audience: REI physicians and reproductive scientists.
Three outcomes matter:(1) live birth, (2) OHSS and safety, (3) any signal in subgroups (PGT-A, ovulatory vs PCOS).
Work in this order and SHOW me each step.
1. PLAN FIRST. Before searching, write a short plan: the exact sub-questions, the study designs that would answer them (prioritise RCTs and meta-analyses of RCTs), inclusion and exclusion rules, and the recency window. Print the plan as a checklist. Do not search until the plan is on screen.
2. FAN OUT. Spawn one subagent per sub-question (no more than four at once) and run them in parallel. Each subagent must:
a. find candidate papers (use the paper-lookup and parallel-web skills; prefer PubMed, Cochrane, and the primary journal),
b. fetch the PRIMARY source, full text or PDF, not a blog and not a secondary summary,
c. extract only the load-bearing numbers: effect size, 95% CI, absolute numbers, n, design,
d. record provenance: DOI and PMID, the exact quoted sentence, and the page or section. Write the pooled result to claims.json, one record per claim.
3. DEBATE. Every claim now goes to TWO independent adversarial verifiers, and they must not share a retrieval path. Both are instructed to REFUTE, not to agree.
Verifier A - Claude Opus 4.8. Spawn a subagent per sub-question. It re-opens the source and tries to show the number is wrong, or right only in a different population than claimed.
Verifier B - OpenAI GPT-5.6-Sol. Run it yourself, from the shell, one call per sub-question, and WAIT for each to finish: codex exec -s workspace-write -c approval_policy=never - < verify_job_N.txt Do NOT pass --effort; the flag is rejected and the correct setting is already the default. Verifier B must retrieve the source ITSELF rather than trusting any excerpt you hand it. That independence is the whole point: two models agreeing after retrieving separately means something, two models agreeing about the same excerpt means nothing.
Each verifier returns, per claim, one of: CONFIRMED - the number appears as stated, in the stated population. Quote the sentence. DISPUTED - it does not. Say precisely what is wrong and quote what the source says. UNRETRIEVABLE - full text could not be obtained. Say what was tried.
4. ADJUDICATE. Tally the two verdicts mechanically. Do not let a model decide this; apply the rule: both CONFIRMED -> keep, tag [verified x2] one CONFIRMED one DISPUTED -> keep ONLY with the disagreement quoted inline, tag [disputed] either UNRETRIEVABLE -> tag [unverified - source not retrieved], and DO NOT USE IT in the bottom line or the summary table Write adjudication.md with a table: Claim | Opus 4.8 | GPT-5.6-Sol | Final | Convergent. Then de-duplicate papers by DOI to PMID, and where studies disagree say so and prefer the stronger design. Note ASRM and ESHRE positions with their year if you find them. If the two models agreed on everything, say so plainly. Convergence is a result, not a failure, and you must never manufacture a disagreement. Make sure to detail primary evidence from original papers and to have gpt and claude debate and marshal evidence for a final judgement on all claims, and make sure that links to primary literature and specific figures therein (examined visually by subagents) are detailed.
The whole thing is published verbatim: the full prompt.
Recorded demo: Claude Code CLI reviews

Prompt

5. DRAW, THEN JUDGE. Generate the explanatory figures, then gate them a. Generate each figure: python3 ~/.claude/skills/generate-image/scripts/generate_image.py "<prompt>" -o figN.png Leave the model at its default. Express size and aspect in the prompt itself; there are no flags for them. b. HARD RULE: a generated figure may carry NO number, NO percentage, and NO data claim. Pictures are for structure and sequence. Every number lives in the table, where it is traceable. If a figure needs a value on it, that is a table, not a picture. c. Judge every figure with BOTH models, each acting as a senior REI physician-scientist, and score it on: no fabricated data; no garbled or misspelled text; anatomical and procedural correctness a practising REI physician or embryologist would accept; legibility when projected. Opus 4.8 reads the file directly. For GPT-5.6-Sol: codex exec -s workspace-write -c approval_policy=never -i figN.png - < judge_job.txt d. Any REJECT or REVISE from either judge means regenerate, at most twice. If it still fails, abandon the AI image and build that figure deterministically instead, in Graphviz or plain HTML and CSS, where you control every label. Log what failed and why in figures_log.md.
6. BUILD. Use /frontend-design skill. Produce explainer.html: ONE self-contained scrolling page, no external network requests, fonts and images inlined as base64, readable on a phone. It must contain, in order: the bottom line - the outcome table (effect sizes, 95% CIs, absolute differences, design, n) - the judged figures - the adjudication table from step 4 - Vancouver-numbered references each tagged [verified x2] or [disputed] or [unverified] - an explicit "what is still uncertain" list - and a short method note naming both models and their versions.
7. WRITE. The prose, and especially the closing summary, is pitched at a SENIOR MD/PhD REI PHYSICIAN-SCIENTIST, not at a general clinician. That means: - Assume fluency in agonist and antagonist protocols, segmentation, VEGF-mediated OHSS pathophysiology, endometrial and embryo synchrony, PGT-A, and cumulative versus per-transfer outcomes. Do not explain what these are.
Give effect sizes with 95% CIs AND absolute risk differences. A relative risk alone is not an answer.
Name the design explicitly - multicentre RCT, meta-analysis of RCTs, registry - report heterogeneity, and where trials disagree, say which population drives the disagreement. - Keep per-transfer and cumulative live birth strictly distinct. Conflating them is the standard error in this literature.
Close on what would change practice, and what evidence would be needed to change it.
Write in long, information-dense sentences that carry their qualifications inside them. Assert directly where the evidence supports it. No em dashes. No "it is worth noting", "importantly", "notably", "delve", "landscape", "robust", "holistic". No throat-clearing, no hedging cascades, and do not set up a gap in the literature just to fill it.
Rules that override everything above: no fabricated citations, numbers, or quotations, ever. If you are unsure, say so in the chat rather than inventing a plausible value. A claim that failed retrieval is reported as unverified and left out, not softened into the text. And do not stage any of this for effect: if nothing was disputed and nothing was rejected, report that honestly.

Embryo AI: accuracy rose, outcome did not

Across 20 retrospective studies, AI out-predicted embryologists: clinical-pregnancy accuracy 77.8% vs 64%, and image-plus-clinical inputs 81.5% vs 51%
Those are prediction accuracies, not clinical outcomes; the evidence was retrospective and not prospectively validated
Salih M, et al. Hum Reprod Open 2023:hoad031. AI vs embryologists (SR). · Illingworth PJ, et al. Nat Med 2024;30:3114-3120. Embryo selection RCT. · Maekawa R, et al. Sci Rep 2026;16:9864. Time-lapse AI.

Embryo AI: accuracy rose, outcome did not

The large double-blind RCT tested the question that matters at transfer: iDAScore gave clinical pregnancy 46.5% vs 48.2% (risk difference −1.7%, p=0.62), and noninferiority was not demonstrated
Live birth was also not improved (39.8% vs 43.5%, p=0.24); the clear win was scoring speed (21 s vs 208 s)
The fix is design: prospective multi-center RCTs with live birth as the endpoint before practice changes
Salih M, et al. Hum Reprod Open 2023:hoad031. AI vs embryologists (SR). · Illingworth PJ, et al. Nat Med 2024;30:3114-3120. Embryo selection RCT. · Maekawa R, et al. Sci Rep 2026;16:9864. Time-lapse AI.

The future
Part 4

The Moving Bottleneck: Where the Hard Problem Lives

AI does not eliminate bottlenecks — it moves them. The next challenge is ensuring what we generate is true.
Part 4

The Future: When Models Meet the World

AI is no longer just a scientific tool but a meta-technology that redefines the very paradigm of discovery
Part 4

Amplify, don't replace

The real prize is workforce survival
Projected shortfall of 11 million health workers by 2030, hardest where disease burden is highest
It is silly to suggest that AI replaces clinicians: ask how it keeps them, expertise amplification, not replacement
Dai T, et al. Lancet 2026. Global advances in health AI: a workforce imperative. · Topol EJ. Daedalus 2026;155:266-276. The future of AI-facilitated medicine.

Part 4

How best to use LLMs

Match the tool to the risk, and the data to the tool
Ground every factual claim in a source, and verify the citation and the number before you reuse it
Keep PHI inside approved, BAA-covered or on-prem systems
Preserve skill through unaided practice and audit

Part 4

Benchmark is not safety

No system earned a safety margin
On 500 MedQA items the tested frontier tier led, Gemini 3.1 Pro 97.4%, GPT-5.2 94.2%, Claude Opus 4.6 90.2%, above the specialized tools OpenEvidence 89.6% and UpToDate 88.4%
On 100 real physician queries scored by 12 blinded clinicians, OpenEvidence (3.24) and UpToDate (3.17 of 4) landed level with a free Google AI Overview (3.27)
Vishwanath K, et al. Nat Med 2026. General-purpose LLMs outperform specialized clinical AI tools.
Part 4

Benchmark is not safety

No system earned a safety margin
Safety did not separate the field: harmful-content and hallucination rates did not differ across systems (Cochran's Q, p=0.55 and p=0.42)
The honest caveat: the benchmark was OpenAI's, the answer-grader was OpenAI's, and a winner was OpenAI's, so a vendor-graded leaderboard is not a safety certificate
Choose by task, auditability, privacy, and independent validation, not by leaderboard rank
Vishwanath K, et al. Nat Med 2026. General-purpose LLMs outperform specialized clinical AI tools.
